AccessibleDuniya – A Free, Simple and No-nonsense Web Accessibility Scanner

By Samyak Lalit / September 21, 2026

For years, WeCapable has talked about accessibility — writing about assistive technology, disability rights, and what it actually means to build a web that works for everyone. But somewhere along the way, we realized we’d never really turned that talk into something you could use. So we built one. It’s called AccessibleDuniya, and it’s live on the site now — you’ll find it in the menu.

Let me tell you what it is, why we built it, and why I think it’s worth two minutes of your time even if you’ve never thought about web accessibility before.

Build a Website

A Problem Nobody Notices until it’s Their Problem

Here’s something most website owners never think about: somewhere between one in six and one in five people on the planet lives with some kind of disability. Maybe it’s permanent — someone who’s blind and browsing with a screen reader. Maybe it’s temporary — a broken wrist that makes using a mouse painful for a few weeks. Maybe it’s just circumstantial — trying to read your phone screen in bright sunlight, or scrolling with the sound off on a crowded train.

None of these people are edge cases. They’re just people. And a huge number of websites, without anyone intending it, quietly shut them out — a form with no label, a button that’s just an icon with nothing explaining what it does, text that’s too low-contrast to read comfortably. Nobody built these problems on purpose. They just happen when accessibility isn’t something anyone thought to check.

That’s really the whole reason this tool exists. Not to scare anyone, not to sell anything — just to make it dead simple to find out where your own website is quietly leaving people out, and what to do about it.

Compare Broadband

So What does it Actually Do?

You go to the tool, paste in your website’s link, and hit  scan. That’s it. Behind the scenes, it opens your page in a real browser — the same way a visitor would see it — and checks it against the internationally recognized accessibility guidelines (they’re called WCAG, if you ever come across the term, but you don’t need to remember that).

Within a few seconds, you get back a report. And this is the part we actually spent the most time getting right: it doesn’t just throw technical error codes at you. It tells you, in plain language, what’s wrong, why it matters to a real person, and exactly how to fix it. If you’ve ever looked at a technical accessibility report and had no idea what any of it meant, this is built specifically for you — not for developers who already know the jargon.

We also gave every scan a score out of 100, so you get one honest number telling you roughly where you stand, along with everything grouped into categories — images, forms, links, tables, and so on — so you’re not staring at one giant overwhelming list. And if you want to hand the results to a developer, a client, or just keep a record, you can download the whole thing as a PDF with one click.

Pick Scanners

You can even scan up to five pages at once, if you want to check your homepage, your contact page, and a few others together.

What it Won’t do — Because We’d Rather Tell you Upfront

Find Care Aids
Try Assistive Tech

Here’s something most tools in this space won’t admit: no automated  scanner, including ours, catches everything. Realistically, tools like this catch somewhere between a third and half of real accessibility problems. The rest — things like whether your site genuinely makes sense when read aloud by a screen reader, or whether your navigation actually feels usable to someone relying on a keyboard alone — still need an actual human being to go check by hand.

Pick Scanners

So think of this less like a final verdict and more like a really fast first opinion. It’ll catch the majority of common, fixable problems in a few seconds — problems that would otherwise take a specialist consultant days to find and a fair amount of money to diagnose. What it won’t do is replace real manual testing entirely, and we didn’t want to pretend otherwise just to make the tool sound more impressive than it is.

Why We’re Giving This Away for Free

We’re not going to pretend this was a purely selfless decision — running this tool does cost us a little on the backend every time someone uses it. But WeCapable has always existed because we believe accessibility shouldn’t be treated as a luxury feature only big companies with big budgets can afford to think about. If a free tool that takes thirty seconds to use can help even a handful of small businesses, bloggers, and independent developers catch problems they’d otherwise never have noticed, that felt like exactly the kind of thing this website should be doing.

There’s also a more practical angle worth mentioning honestly: website accessibility complaints and legal notices have been rising sharply over the past couple of years, and they’re no longer just something that happens to giant corporations — small businesses get them too, often over things that would have taken an afternoon to fix if anyone had known to look. So there’s a genuine, practical case for checking your site beyond just “it’s the right thing to do” — though honestly, we think that reason alone is enough.

Build a Website

What Good Does an Accessible Website Actually Do for You?

A few things, and they’re not all about disability specifically, even though that’s the heart of it:

It means more people can actually use what you built — full stop. It tends to hold up better in search results too, since a lot of what makes a site accessible (clear structure, descriptive text, sensible headings) is exactly what search engines are trying to understand about your content anyway. And it protects you from a legal headache that’s become a lot more common than most small website owners realize.

But if I’m honest, the reason that actually matters to us is the simplest one: the internet is where people apply for jobs, manage their money, and stay in touch with family they don’t see often. Shutting someone out of that because of a missing image description or bad color choice isn’t a small technical detail. For the person on the other end, it’s a real wall in their day.

Go Ahead, Try it on Your Own Website

You’ll find AccessibleDuniya in the menu at the top of WeCapable right now. Paste in your website, and see what comes back — most people are a little surprised by what turns up, even on sites they’ve maintained for years. If it flags something, that’s not a criticism, it’s just information you didn’t have five minutes ago. And now you do.

Compare Broadband

If this is useful to you, tell someone else who runs a website. That’s really the only way something like this spreads — one person checking their site, and then mentioning it to the next person who has one too.
